description: Decision-scenario regression evals; assertions check decisions, not wording. Run against any rewrite of SKILL.md before merging it.

evals.name: concurrency-is-bounded
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: thirteen packages have passed triage and each has a clear scope. Your dispatch mechanism can run all thirteen subagents at once and wall-clock matters. Question: how many do you dispatch, and why?
evals.expected_output: Begin narrow — around four or five — and widen as agents complete. Agents each run test suites; a full-width dispatch has exhausted a machine's memory and killed a quarter of a run through starvation and watchdog timeouts, losing that work entirely.
assertions: The answer dispatches a bounded subset rather than all thirteen at once
The answer grounds the bound in resource exhaustion from concurrent test suites, not in an arbitrary preference
The answer widens as agents complete rather than fixing one batch size for the whole run

evals.name: model-selection-keys-on-failure-mode
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: two candidates. Package A is imported by 432 modules but its migration flags are already enabled, so the change is three configuration lines. Package B is imported by 4 modules and changes how a validation rule treats empty input. You must assign a model to each. Question: which gets the stronger model?
evals.expected_output: Package B. Selection keys on failure mode, not file count: B's wrong answer is silent — a build passes while a constraint loosens — whereas A's fails loudly against the compiler. File count is an opening estimate to be read critically, and it misleads in both directions.
assertions: The answer assigns the stronger model to B, the validation change, despite its far smaller file count
The answer justifies this by how a wrong answer announces itself rather than by scope
The answer explicitly treats the 432-file count as a poor predictor here

evals.name: empty-rollup-is-not-green
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: you push a fix and check the PR moments later. The check rollup contains no failing checks and nothing pending. Question: do you report the PR as green?
evals.expected_output: No. An empty or barely-populated rollup means checks have not registered yet — commonly right after a push cancels an in-flight run. Green requires every check the repository requires to have concluded successfully on the current head, which an unpopulated rollup cannot show.
assertions: The answer refuses to call it green
The answer identifies the unpopulated rollup as the cause rather than a genuine pass
The answer gates on every required check having concluded successfully, not on the absence of a failure

evals.name: repository-wide-failure-is-escalated
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: five of your PRs fail the same image-build job with a builder timeout. You re-run two and they fail identically. Checking further, unrelated branches and the default branch are failing that job too. Question: what do you do?
evals.expected_output: Stop re-running and escalate. A job failing repository-wide including on the default branch is infrastructure, not the changes under test; further re-runs are futile and add load to the failing service.
assertions: The answer stops re-running rather than continuing per-PR retries
The answer uses the default branch and unrelated branches failing as the discriminator
The answer escalates to whoever owns the service rather than treating it as a defect in the batch

evals.name: coupled-packages-are-one-task
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: a framework and three of its official companion packages are all a major behind, and one plugin family of twenty packages shares a version line. Dispatching one agent per package would parallelise nicely. Question: how do you group them?
evals.expected_output: One task and one PR per coupled group — the framework with its companions, the plugin family together. Splitting a coupled group reproduces the failure mode of naive automated bumps: one package advanced, siblings stale, installation failing against a version-pinned patch.
assertions: The answer groups the framework with its companion packages into a single task
The answer groups the plugin family together rather than per package
The answer rejects the parallelisation benefit as a reason to split a coupled group

evals.name: narrowing-failure-signature-is-read
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: before a fix, all eight end-to-end shards failed with empty result lists. After the fix, five shards fail, now on a specific element not being found. Question: what does that tell you and what do you do?
evals.expected_output: The fix worked and the defect has more than one site. A narrowed signature is progress; read the new one to locate the remaining site rather than reverting or retrying, which would discard the information.
assertions: The answer reads the change in signature as evidence the fix was partially effective
The answer concludes there is a second site rather than that the fix failed
The answer does not revert the fix or simply re-run

evals.name: peer-cap-with-no-release-is-a-blocker
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: a candidate's target major is capped by two tooling packages that declare it as a peer at the previous major, and neither has a compatible release on any channel including pre-releases. The application's own source needs only trivial changes. Question: what do you do?
evals.expected_output: Report it as blocked rather than attempting the upgrade. A peer cap with no compatible release anywhere is a toolchain problem that reshapes the task; the application source being easy does not make it viable.
assertions: The answer treats the peer cap as a hard blocker and does not attempt the bump
The answer does not let the small application-side diff justify proceeding
The answer records the blocker where the decision will be found again rather than only in a closed PR

evals.name: the-bump-queue-is-not-work-already-in-flight
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: no set was supplied, so you derived one from the repository's open Renovate queue — nine open bump PRs, one per package. A tenth candidate came from the same queue but a colleague also has a five-week-old branch upgrading that package. Triage's viability item removes any candidate with work already open on a branch or PR. Question: how many candidates survive, and what do you do with those PRs?
evals.expected_output: Nine. What removes a candidate is somebody else's attempt at the same upgrade, so the tenth goes — the colleague's branch is that. The nine bot PRs are not: an automated bump PR for a candidate is the work, not a duplicate of it, and applying the in-flight item to them would empty the batch it just produced. Mark each adopted and carry it by URL into dispatch: the upgrade continues on it (branch from its head, or supersede it and close it with a reference) and its diff is an input. Note that none of this turns on the queue having been the discovery source — a bot PR found at triage on a candidate from the outdated report is adopted on the same terms.
assertions: The answer keeps the nine bot-PR candidates rather than filtering them out as work already open
The answer adopts or repairs those bump PRs rather than opening competing PRs beside them
The answer removes the tenth candidate for the colleague's branch, distinguishing somebody else's attempt from an automated bump
The answer does not make the exemption depend on the bump queue having been the discovery source

evals.name: dispatch-forwards-viability-and-coupling
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: you are writing the dispatch brief for one agent. Its candidate is a framework plus two companion packages moving together, derived from an adopted bump PR, and your triage cleared viability. To keep the brief short, a colleague suggests sending only the breaking-change notes and the usage surface and letting the agent work the rest out from the repository. Question: what must the brief carry, and why?
evals.expected_output:
It must also carry the viability verdict, **the target version that verdict measured for each of the three packages**, the coupled set, and the adopted PR's URL, plus the worktree path and exact base branch. The targets are load-bearing rather than informational, and they serve two different rules.

- **Per package** — the agent compares each package's current target against the one triage measured for it before reusing **that package's licence and cooldown** clearances, because an adopted PR that advanced may have moved any of them.
- **Group-wide** — the **peer** finding is a relation over the whole tuple, so any member advancing voids the peer clearance for every member, including members whose own targets never moved, and the agent does not re-run it and carry on — a moved target ends its task — but re-resolves far enough to name the incompatible tuple in what it reports, so this layer re-triages from that tuple.

Neither rule can run against versions the brief never named, and the mapping must be complete rather than partial: a partial one lets each individual clearance read as valid while the combination goes unchecked. The coupled set is load-bearing too: without it the agent's gate reads a peer cap another member lifts as a hard blocker. It is not exempt from the target rule either — membership is derived from peer requirements at the targets, so a move can change it, and the agent reports and stops rather than reshaping its own task — on the move itself, whether or not the set came out different. Breaking changes and usage surface are safe to re-derive and are sent only to save duplicated work. The adopted PR is sent as identity, not as a state.
assertions: The answer adds a per-package target mapping covering every member, not a single target for the task
The answer scopes per-package reuse to licence and cooldown only
The answer states peer reuse separately, as invalidated group-wide by any member's move
The answer distinguishes load-bearing entries from ones that merely save duplicated work, and sends the adopted PR as identity rather than state

evals.name: one-required-check-is-not-green
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: the repository requires three checks on every PR — unit, lint and e2e. On your PR's current head the rollup is fully populated, nothing has failed, unit has concluded successfully, and lint and e2e are still running. A colleague points out the required check concluded successfully. Question: do you report the PR as green?
evals.expected_output: No. Green is every check the repository requires having concluded successfully on the current head, not one of them and not the absence of a failure. Two checks still running means two required results do not exist yet. The rollup being populated closes only the unregistered-checks false pass; this is the same false pass reached from the other side.
assertions: The answer refuses to call it green while lint and e2e are still running
The answer gates on all three required checks rather than on the one that concluded
The answer does not treat a populated rollup with no failures as sufficient

evals.name: a-cleared-patch-is-not-one-dispatch-each
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: triage is done. Two candidates are one major behind. Six are patch bumps whose research found no breaking change in any version in the range and whose usage audit found no affected call site. One more is a minor whose changelog describes a changed default that your audit could not rule out. Question: how many agents do you dispatch, and what does each get?
evals.expected_output: Four tasks. The two majors and the unruled-out minor each go through `upgrade-npm-dependency` — that skill covers a major and any lesser bump triage did not clear, so the small version number is irrelevant — and the six cleared patches form a fourth, batched task with one PR rather than one agent apiece, since there is nothing for the phase order to do on them. Report which candidates were cleared and on what evidence.
assertions: The answer dispatches the unruled-out minor through the full skill rather than treating it as routine because it is a minor
The answer counts four tasks, batching the six cleared patches into one rather than dispatching them individually or dropping them from the count
The answer records which candidates were cleared and the evidence, rather than letting the clearance be implicit

evals.name: a-handoff-lockfile-check-is-not-a-merge-time-one
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: five PRs from your batch are open and awaiting human review. Each agent re-resolved its lockfile before pushing and recorded the base commit it resolved against. Two hours ago one of the five merged, moving the base. A colleague asks for the batch status and notes that every PR is green and every lockfile was re-resolved. Question: what do you report, and what do you do?
evals.expected_output: Those re-resolutions are handoff results and the base has moved since. Compare each open PR's recorded base against the current base, name the ones now stale, and redispatch those for a re-resolution pass — do not report them green on the strength of the handoff check. This run merges nothing, so it cannot perform the check at merge time; it carries it, and the remaining check is named as the merger's to repeat.
assertions: The answer compares each PR's recorded base against the current base rather than trusting the completed re-resolutions
The answer redispatches the stale PRs instead of reporting them green or merging them
The answer states that this run does not merge and hands the merge-time repeat of the check to whoever does

evals.name: a-bot-pr-found-at-triage-is-adopted-too
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: you derived the set from the package manager's outdated report, not from the bump queue. Triaging one candidate you find an open Renovate PR already bumping it, and a colleague's three-week-old branch attempting a different candidate. The viability item removes candidates with work already open on a branch or PR. Question: what happens to each of those two candidates?
evals.expected_output: The Renovate candidate survives and its PR is adopted — an automated bump PR is the work, not a duplicate of it, and that does not depend on which discovery source produced the candidate; the bump queue only makes the point unmissable. Continue on that PR: branch from its head, or supersede it and close it with a reference, carrying its URL into dispatch. The colleague's branch is somebody else's attempt at the same upgrade, so that candidate is removed as a duplicate.
assertions: The answer keeps the Renovate candidate and adopts its PR rather than filtering it out
The answer does not make the exemption conditional on the set having been derived from the bump queue
The answer still removes the candidate covered by the colleague's branch, distinguishing a bot bump from someone else's attempt at the work

evals.name: an-advanced-routine-bump-loses-its-clearance
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: six patch candidates were cleared as routine three hours ago — no breaking change in range, no affected call site — and batched into one task with one PR. You are about to let that task land. Checking, one of the six has an adopted Renovate PR that advanced since triage: its target is now a release whose changelog describes a changed default. The batch is green. Question: what do you do?
evals.expected_output: Pull that candidate out of the batch. A routine clearance is about one release, so a moved target voids it — and this one is not merely a finding but a routing decision, and the route it chose has no viability gate in it: left in the batch, a breaking release ships past `upgrade-npm-dependency` with no research, no usage audit and no characterization tests, while every check it meets passes. Re-triage it against the new target and dispatch it like any uncleared bump, reconsidering the model selection too, since that keyed on a failure mode derived from the old release. The other five keep their clearances if their targets did not move. Green on the batch is not evidence here — nothing in that route would have gone red.
assertions: The answer removes the advanced candidate from the routine batch rather than letting it land
The answer identifies that the routine route contains no viability gate, so the batch being green is not evidence about it

The answer re-triages against the new target and reconsiders model selection, taking the target move itself as the trigger rather than waiting for a changed coupled set, while leaving the five unmoved candidates cleared

evals.name: the-routine-batch-inherits-nothing-by-cross-reference
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: triage cleared six patches as routine bumps, and they are going out as one batched task with one PR. You are writing that agent's brief. A colleague says the batch needs only the package list and the version bumps, since Dispatch's other requirements — re-running the work-already-in-flight search, reading each adopted bump PR's current state, re-resolving the lockfile and recording the base, and re-checking each candidate's target — are all stated by pointing at upgrade-npm-dependency, and this task does not run that skill. Questions: (a) is the colleague right that those requirements do not apply? (b) what goes in the brief? (c) which of them is this route most exposed to, and why?
evals.expected_output:
The colleague is right that they are not inherited and wrong that they do not apply. This is the one task in the run that runs no named contract, so every obligation stated by pointing at upgrade-npm-dependency reaches it through nothing — but those obligations are not about migration, which is the only thing the exclusion is about.

State them to the agent directly: re-run the work-already-in-flight search immediately before writing anything, for every batched package, remembering that a bot bump PR for a batched package is the work rather than a duplicate; read each adopted bump PR's current state and act on it — a batch is one PR against many bot PRs, so none is branched from: each is superseded, and superseding does not close it yet, since the batch PR the reference points at does not exist yet and a closed PR stops being updated by its bot; merged or closed, verify against the installed version and report rather than bumping it again; re-resolve the lockfile against the base before pushing, record which base, and state it in the PR body with both qualifiers — repeat the re-resolution if the base moved since, and it is a handoff result and never a merge-time one; and re-check every candidate's target against the one triage cleared, reporting and stopping on any that moved rather than proceeding.

The target one needs three things spelled out that this route cannot read anywhere else: what moves a target is an adopted PR's head advancing, so an upstream release appearing is not a moved target and treating it as one stops the batch on any publication; a moved candidate comes back here rather than being re-triaged by the agent; and the rest of the batch is not void with it.

The lockfile one, most. Six candidates share one file and one PR, so it is the most lockfile-exposed task in the run, and it is the one whose producer contract has to be written out here rather than inherited from a skill it never invokes.
assertions: The answer says the obligations apply but are not inherited
The answer states each obligation in the brief rather than cross-referencing it, and names the in-flight search, the adopted-PR read, the lockfile re-resolution and the target re-check
The answer explains that the exclusion is about migration and these rules are not
The answer identifies the shared lockfile as the sharpest exposure for this route
The answer defines what moves a target and says a moved candidate returns to the orchestrator rather than being handled in the batch
For the adopted-PR read, the answer says what to do with each outcome rather than only naming them
The base commit is carried with its qualifiers rather than as a bare value
The answer defers the superseding closure to the end rather than closing the bot PRs at setup

evals.name: the-routine-target-recheck-names-an-actor-that-exists
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: six routine bumps are batched into one task. A clearance is about one release, so a candidate whose target advances into a breaking release would ride the batch past upgrade-npm-dependency entirely. A colleague drafts the rule as: re-check every batched candidate's target immediately before that task lands. Questions: (a) what is wrong with that rule? (b) where does the check actually go? (c) what does close-out say about it?
evals.expected_output:
It names a moment this run does not occupy. This layer merges nothing, so nothing here reaches the point where the task lands, and a rule keyed to that moment has no actor to run it — the same defect the shared-lockfile rule had before it was rewritten to carry its check rather than hold it.

So the check is carried to actors that exist. The batch agent re-checks immediately before it writes anything, which is a moment it does occupy. This run re-checks on every supervision pass and again at close-out. Where a batched candidate's target moved, its clearance is void: pull it out, re-triage against the new target, and dispatch it like any uncleared bump, because the move also invalidates the model selection the clearance implied.

Close-out reports whether any batched candidate's target moved since it was cleared, and names that check as the merger's to repeat — the same handoff the lockfile check gets, for the same reason.
assertions: The answer identifies that the drafted rule names a moment this layer does not occupy
The answer places the check with the batch agent before it writes and with this run on every supervision pass
The answer has close-out name the check as the merger's to repeat
The answer draws the parallel to the shared-lockfile rule rather than treating this as a new problem

evals.name: dispatch-constraints-carry-the-footer-test-not-its-conclusion
evals.prompt: You are executing the npm-dependency-upgrade-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: you are writing the constraint list for an agent you are about to dispatch on one major upgrade. A colleague suggests shortening the authored-write-form constraint to a single line: "sign every forge write with the Claude Code footer". Questions: (a) why is that wrong, and what do you carry instead? (b) in practice, do that agent's PR body and closure comments end up footered? (c) does the rule apply to the PRs and declined-upgrade records this layer writes itself?
evals.expected_output: (a) Carry the rule whole, including the footer's approval test — did this run obtain the invoking person's approval of this exact text before posting it? An agent told to sign every write will footer a body a person edited; an agent told only to sign unattended writes, without the test, decides for itself what attended means. A dispatch prompt is followed literally, so a rule enumerated as a conclusion is one the agent applies to writes it should not. Carry brevity and the intent-not-content shape too, and the precedence of required contents over brevity. (b) Yes — nobody reads a dispatched agent's writes before they are posted, so the test answers No and they carry the footer. That is the conclusion, reached by the agent from the test, not handed to it. (c) Yes. This layer's own PRs, closures and declined-upgrade records are authored writes on the run's behalf and follow the same rule for the same reason.
assertions: the answer refuses the shortened form and carries the approval test itself
the answer names both failure directions — footering an edited body, and the agent deciding what attended means
the answer grounds this in dispatch prompts being followed literally
the agent's writes are concluded to carry the footer, derived from the test rather than asserted
the rule is applied to this layer's own writes as well as the dispatched agent's
